If a bagless prototype already worked, why redevelop it overseas, then return to in-house manufacturing and early British retail orders? Follow factory powder clogging a cloth filter, the diagnosis of a household bag's pores, cardboard and metal prototypes, licensing and joint Japanese development, then tooling finance, rented assembly space, mail-order demonstrations and in-store explanations.

A licensed British Cyclon product existed before Japan; 1983–84 and 550 units come from Dyson's recollection. Italian manufacture applies only to the museum's individual object. Japan is not described as the first market worldwide. The 1985 Nishi-Azabu head-redesign photo, the recalled 1986 agreement with Apex and the Japanese launch are separate records, not grounds for backdating a contract. M+'s 1983/Silver Seiko, V&A's 1986/APEX and the Science Museum Group's 1985–1990/Apex are different collection fields, not one record of a first sale or manufacturing contract.

New material comes from original interview publication pages, the company biography and Robin Roy's interview research. Masters of Scale labels its official transcript as automatically generated and not fully corrected; the author has not separately listened to the audio, and the relevant details still await independent source review. The new bank recollection differs from the older Fortune account in dates and currencies, so the narration uses only the internal appeal and house collateral, without combining them into a precise year and amount. The half-factory interview supplies no location or date and cannot be equated with Bumpers Farm in 1993. The dry-powder demonstration applies the accompanying powder before vacuuming; it is not evidence of wet pickup or a general performance test. The advertising-for-orders deal is another undated recollection of early British distribution, not the same transaction with the first mail-order buyer.
